questions.title: How did the indictment satisfy § 1348’s “money or property” requirement without invoking the discredited right-to-control theory?
questions.question_body: The panel says Ciminelli bars convictions based solely on depriving victims of valuable economic information, but upholds this indictment because it alleges fraudulent inducement to part with money. I’m struggling to see the property interest here: the followers bought market-traded securities (arguably at then-market prices), and there was no alleged right-to-control theory. Is the idea that the victims’ cash used to buy shares is the protected property, even if they received securities of equal value at the time? What makes this different from simply providing (allegedly false) information that affects someone’s decision-making, which Ciminelli seemed to reject?

questions.title: How does the fraudulent-inducement theory apply when victims purchase on an open market from unknown counterparties?
questions.question_body: Kousisis involved a contract directly induced by misrepresentations, making it easy to see how the defendant “obtained” the victim’s money. Here, purchases occurred on public markets. The opinion says defendants pumped and then dumped, but not every induced buyer necessarily bought from a defendant. Does § 1348 require that the defendant actually obtain the particular victim’s money, or is it enough that some investors were induced to buy and defendants monetized the inflated price by selling into that demand? How does the government satisfy the “obtain money or property” element in a dispersed open-market setting?

questions.title: Post-Kousisis, does the Fifth Circuit still require an intent to cause economic harm, or only an intent to obtain money through deception?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Evans for intent to defraud as intent to deceive and intent to cause harm, but then relies on Kousisis to say no net loss is required and it’s enough that defendants had “money in mind.” How are courts reconciling Evans’s “harm” prong with Kousisis? Is “harm” now satisfied whenever the object is to obtain money by deceit, even if the plan doesn’t contemplate leaving the victim worse off on a net basis?

questions.title: Are predictions about a stock’s “potential price” actionable misrepresentations at the indictment stage, or are they non-actionable puffery/opinion?
questions.question_body: The indictment mentions posts misrepresenting trading positions and the potential price of securities. I understand that lying about one’s present trading position is a statement of fact, but statements about future price often look like opinion or puffery. At the Rule 12 stage, does the court simply assume materiality and falsity for both types of statements, or is there a doctrinal line about when optimistic price predictions can support a § 1348 charge?

questions.title: What is the scope of § 1348’s “in connection with” requirement and do social-media posts satisfy it without a transactional relationship?
questions.question_body: The statute requires a scheme to defraud “in connection with” the purchase or sale of a security. Here, the alleged misstatements were public social-media posts rather than direct solicitations to identified buyers. How tight must the nexus be? Is it sufficient that the posts were intended to induce trading activity generally, or does the government need to allege a closer link to specific purchases or sales?

questions.title: Why proceed under § 1348 instead of § 10(b)/Rule 10b-5, and what elements differ in the criminal context (e.g., reliance, loss causation)?
questions.question_body: The conduct sounds like classic pump-and-dump manipulation often charged under § 10(b) and Rule 10b-5, but this case proceeds under § 1348. Does § 1348 avoid civil-law concepts like reliance and loss causation that sometimes appear in § 10(b) cases? In a criminal § 1348 prosecution, what must the government prove about materiality, causation, or market impact compared to a Rule 10b-5 theory?

questions.title: What exactly must an indictment allege under Rule 12 to survive a motion to dismiss for failure to state an offense?
questions.question_body: The court emphasizes taking the indictment’s allegations as true and only checking for the material elements. In practical terms, could defendants argue at this stage that the followers got fair value or that posts were not actually misleading, or are those purely trial issues? How specific must the indictment be about the mechanics of the scheme (who bought from whom, timing of trades, which posts were false) to provide fair notice and double-jeopardy protection under Fifth Circuit standards?
